# Outline

- Mixed response types: modelling communities with different measurement scales
- Spatial and temporal autocorrelation in latent variables
- Case study: joint modelling across survey methods with spatial and temporal structure

## Questions so far?

\center

![](../questions.jpg){width=40%}

# Mixed responses

## Not all species are measured the same way

Community data rarely comes in a single format:

- Species composition: presence-absence
- Dominant grasses: % cover
- Rare forbs: count of individuals
- Invertebrates: biomass

\pause

Standard GLLVMs fit one distribution to all species. But forcing binary, count, and continuous responses into the same family means either:

- \textbf{Information loss} (discretising continuous data)
- \textbf{Model misspecification} (Poisson for proportion data)

## Mixed response GLLVMs

In `gllvm`, the `family` argument accepts a \textbf{character vector} of length $p$ (one per species column):

```{r}
family_vec <- c(rep("binomial", 12), rep("poisson", 8), rep("tweedie", 4))

fit <- gllvm(y = Y, family = family_vec, num.lv = 2)
```

\pause

Each species gets its own link function and variance structure. The latent variables $\mathbf{u}_i$ are shared across all species.

## What distributions are available?

\begin{table}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{p{3.0cm}p{3.8cm}p{1.6cm}}
\toprule
Family & Data type & Link \\
\midrule
\texttt{"gaussian"} & Continuous, symmetric & identity \\
\texttt{"tweedie"} & Non-negative, zero-inflated & log \\
\texttt{"orderedBeta"} & Proportions including 0/1 & logit \\
\texttt{"betaH"} & Proportions excluding 0 or 1 & logit \\
\texttt{"poisson"} & Counts & log \\
\texttt{"negative.binomial"} & Overdispersed counts & log \\
\texttt{"binomial"} & Presence-absence or trials & probit \\
\texttt{"ZIP"}, \texttt{"ZINB"} & Zero-inflated counts & log \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

## Why the latent variable framework makes this possible

The GLLVM is species-specific in its response model:

$$g_j(\mu_{ij}) = \beta_{0j} + \mathbf{x}_i^\top \symbf{\beta}_j + \mathbf{u}_i^\top \symbf{\gamma}_j$$

but the latent variables $\mathbf{u}_i$ are \textbf{shared}: they represent the underlying community state at site $i$.

\pause

Different families for different $j$ is just a change in $g_j(\cdot)$ and the variance function; the ordination structure is unaffected.

\pause

This is what makes joint modelling across survey methods possible.

## Binomial with $N > 1$ trials

When species are recorded as frequencies (e.g., Raunkiaer: $k$ quadrats occupied out of $N = 100$):

```{r}
fit <- gllvm(y = Y, family = "binomial", Ntrials = 100, num.lv = 2)
```

`Ntrials` can also be a vector of length $p$ if trials differ per species, or a matrix of size $n \times p$.

\pause

Default link for binomial in `gllvm` is \textbf{probit}, not logit.

## orderedBeta for proportions

Proportions including exact 0 and 1 (e.g., Braun-Blanquet cover converted to $[0,1]$):

```{r}
fit <- gllvm(y = Y / 100, family = "orderedBeta", num.lv = 2)
```

The orderedBeta distribution places point masses at 0 and 1 with a Beta distribution on $(0, 1)$. More appropriate than `"beta"` when true absences and full cover both occur.

\pause

`zetacutoff` controls the quantile threshold for the zero/one mixture; default is usually fine, but set explicitly for stability:

```{r}
fit <- gllvm(..., family = "orderedBeta", zetacutoff = c(-2, 2))
```

## Combining families in a single model

A realistic community dataset might need:

```{r}
family_vec <- ifelse(grepl("_cover$", colnames(Y)), "orderedBeta",
              ifelse(grepl("_count$", colnames(Y)), "negative.binomial",
                                                    "binomial"))

Ntrials <- ifelse(grepl("_freq$", colnames(Y)), 100, 1)

fit <- gllvm(y      = Y,
             family = family_vec,
             Ntrials = Ntrials,
             num.lv = 2,
             zetacutoff = c(-2, 2))
```

## What does a joint model across datasets look like?

Two surveys, different methods, stacked as rows:

- Rows 1--$n_1$: survey A (ordinal columns only)
- Rows $n_1 + 1$--$n_1 + n_2$: survey B (binomial columns only)
- Shared species appear twice: `_COV` and `_FREQ` columns, with `NA` in the opposite block

\pause

The model estimates \textbf{one set of latent variables} covering all rows, and \textbf{separate loadings} for `_COV` and `_FREQ` versions of each shared species.

\pause

If the methods agree, $\hat{\symbf{\gamma}}_{j,\text{COV}} \approx \hat{\symbf{\gamma}}_{j,\text{FREQ}}$; testable with cosine similarity or Procrustes.

# Spatial and temporal autocorrelation

## A core assumption we have not questioned

All GLLVMs so far assume sites are \textbf{independent} after conditioning on the latent variables and covariates.

$$\mathbf{u}_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_d)$$

\pause

This fails when:

- Plots are close in space and share unmeasured environmental variation
- The same plots are revisited over time
- The design has nested structure (transects within sites)

## Structured covariance for the latent variables

Replace independent LV draws with a \textbf{correlated} distribution:

$$\mathbf{u}_{.q} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \symbf{\Sigma}_q), \quad q = 1, \ldots, d$$

where $\symbf{\Sigma}_q$ encodes the dependence structure.

\pause

In `gllvm`: argument `lvCor` specifies the covariance model; `studyDesign` provides the grouping or ordering variable.

## Structures available in gllvm

\begin{table}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{p{3.2cm}p{2.8cm}p{2.8cm}}
\toprule
Formula syntax & Structure & Use case \\
\midrule
\texttt{\textasciitilde corAR1(1|time)} & AR(1) & Equally-spaced time series \\
\texttt{\textasciitilde corExp(1|site)} & Exponential kernel & Spatial data (coordinate-based) \\
\texttt{\textasciitilde corMatern(1|site)} & Matérn kernel & Spatial data (smoother fields) \\
\texttt{\textasciitilde corCS(1|group)} & Compound symmetry & Nested designs \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The same structures are available for row effects via `row.eff`.

\vspace{0.4em}
\footnotesize You have seen \texttt{lvCor} before for nested designs (\texttt{corCS}); the same argument accepts spatial and temporal kernels.

## Temporal autocorrelation: AR(1)

Community composition at time $t$ is correlated with time $t-1$:

$$\symbf{\Sigma}_q[t, t'] = \rho^{|t - t'|}, \quad \rho \in (-1, 1)$$

```{r}
fit_ar1 <- gllvm(
  y           = Y,
  X           = Xenv,
  formula     = ~ temperature + precipitation,
  num.lv      = 2,
  studyDesign = data.frame(site = site_id, year = year_id),
  row.eff     = ~corAR1(1|year),
  lvCor       = ~corAR1(1|year),
  family      = "negative.binomial"
)
fit_ar1$params$rho.lv   # estimated temporal correlation
```

## Spatial autocorrelation: corExp

Correlation decays exponentially with geographic distance:

$$\symbf{\Sigma}_q[i, k] = \exp\!\left(-\frac{d_{ik}}{\rho}\right)$$

$\rho$ is the \textbf{range parameter}: the distance at which correlation has decayed to $e^{-1} \approx 0.37$.

\pause

Effective range (correlation $< 0.05$): $d \approx 3\rho$.

```{r}
fit_sp <- gllvm(
  y           = Y,
  num.lv      = 2,
  distLV      = site_coords,    # n x 2 coordinate matrix
  lvCor       = ~corExp(1|site),
  studyDesign = data.frame(site = site_id),
  family      = "orderedBeta"
)
fit_sp$params$rho.lv   # range in same units as site_coords
```

## Spatial vs. temporal: which to use?

\columnsbegin
\column{0.48\textwidth}
\textbf{Row effects} (\texttt{row.eff})

Community-level variation: affects all species equally at a site.

Good for: site productivity, observer effects, year-level abundance shifts.
\column{0.48\textwidth}
\textbf{LV correlation} (\texttt{lvCor})

Species composition variation: different species respond differently to the latent gradient.

Good for: spatially or temporally structured community turnover.
\columnsend

\pause

\vspace{0.5em}
Both can be included simultaneously:

```{r}
fit <- gllvm(...,
  row.eff = ~corAR1(1|year),
  lvCor   = ~corExp(1|site))
```

## The Matérn covariance

A more flexible spatial kernel:

$$K(d) = \sigma^2 \frac{2^{1-\nu}}{\Gamma(\nu)}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2\nu}\, d}{\rho}\right)^\nu \mathcal{K}_\nu\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{2\nu}\, d}{\rho}\right)$$

- $\nu = 1/2$ recovers the exponential kernel
- Higher $\nu$ produces smoother spatial fields
- $\nu$ is typically fixed (hard to estimate); common choices: $1/2$, $3/2$, $5/2$

\pause

Use `corMatern` when you expect smooth spatial gradients rather than abrupt local variation.

## Computational considerations

Spatial/temporal GLLVMs require inverting $\symbf{\Sigma}_q$, which is expensive for large $n$.

\pause

`gllvm` uses \textbf{sparse approximations} to the variational covariance matrix:

- `Lambda.struc = "bdNN"`: block-diagonal nearest-neighbour Cholesky
- `Lambda.struc = "UNN"`: Kronecker product with NN sparse Cholesky

`NN` controls the number of neighbours; more neighbours = better approximation, slower fitting.

\pause

For large datasets ($n > 500$), start with `NN = 5` and increase if needed.

## Concurrent ordination with covariates

Yesterday we saw \textbf{concurrent ordination}: LVs constrained to be linear combinations of predictors.

With `num.lv.c` and `lv.formula`, we can combine this with spatial/temporal structure:

```{r}
fit_conc <- gllvm(
  y          = Y,
  X          = X,
  family     = "poisson",
  num.lv.c   = 2,
  lv.formula = ~ temperature + moisture,
  distLV     = site_coords,
  lvCor      = ~corExp(1|site),
  studyDesign = data.frame(site = site_id),
  randomB    = "LV"
)
```

The LVs are simultaneously informed by covariates and spatially correlated.

# Case study, Garchinger Heide

```{r garchinger-load, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(gllvm)
library(vegan)
source("load_garchinger_heide_gllvm.R")
load("fit3.RData")   # unconstrained joint model
load("fit4.RData")   # + spatial corExp on LVs
load("fit5.RData")   # + Year as concurrent covariate
```

```{r garchinger-results, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
rho_m <- fit4$params$rho.lv * 1000
eff_m <- round(-rho_m * log(0.05))

gamma_sp <- getLoadings(fit4)
lc       <- gamma_sp[col_cov,     , drop = FALSE]
lf       <- gamma_sp[col_fshared, , drop = FALSE]
rownames(lc) <- rownames(lf) <- shared$freq[ord_shared]
set.seed(1)
pt     <- vegan::protest(lc, lf, permutations = 999)
pr_cor <- round(pt$t0, 2)
pr_p   <- formatC(pt$signif, digits = 3, format = "f")

gamma_t <- getLoadings(fit5)
lc5     <- gamma_t[col_cov,     , drop = FALSE]
lf5     <- gamma_t[col_fshared, , drop = FALSE]
rownames(lc5) <- rownames(lf5) <- shared$freq[ord_shared]
set.seed(1)
pt5      <- vegan::protest(lc5, lf5, permutations = 999)
pr_cor_5 <- round(pt5$t0, 2)

aic_tab <- AIC(fit3, fit4, fit5)
```

## Families used in the Garchinger case study

\begin{table}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{p{2.8cm}p{4.0cm}p{1.6cm}}
\toprule
Family & Data type & Link \\
\midrule
\texttt{"ordinal"} & Ordered categories (Londo / BB codes) & cumulative probit \\
\texttt{"ZNIB"} & Zero-inflated count, $N$ trials & log \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\pause

\texttt{zeta.struc = "common"}: cutpoints shared across species. Species-specific cutpoints (\texttt{"species"}) are unidentifiable under a block-diagonal NA structure.

## The Garchinger Heide dataset

A calcareous grassland in Bavaria (Bauer \& Albrecht 2020, *Basic and Applied Ecology*; data: PANGAEA).

\vspace{0.5em}

Two long-term monitoring programmes, never combined before:

\vspace{0.5em}

\columnsbegin
\column{0.48\textwidth}
\textbf{Coverage survey}

42 plots $\times$ \{2003, 2018\}

Londo ordinal codes (12 levels)

$\to$ ordinal
\column{0.48\textwidth}
\textbf{Frequency survey}

40 plots $\times$ \{1984, 1993, 2018\}

Raunkiaer (/100 quadrats)

$\to$ ZNIB, $N = 100$
\columnsend

\vspace{0.5em}

**Question:** do the two methods recover the same community gradient?

## The joint model design

Stack both surveys as rows; shared species get two columns:

\vspace{0.3em}

\begin{table}
\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{p{2.5cm}p{2.2cm}p{2.2cm}p{2.2cm}}
\toprule
 & \texttt{Bromus\_COV} & \texttt{Bromus\_FREQ} & \texttt{Molinia\_FREQ} \\
\midrule
COV, plot S03, 2003 & 5 & \texttt{NA} & \texttt{NA} \\
COV, plot S03, 2018 & 7 & \texttt{NA} & \texttt{NA} \\
FREQ, plot II5, 1984 & \texttt{NA} & 73 & 12 \\
FREQ, plot II5, 2018 & \texttt{NA} & 81 & 8 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\vspace{0.3em}

- 204 rows, 196 columns; 79 shared species $\times$ 2 + survey-only
- Block-diagonal NA structure: no plot is in both surveys

## The identification problem

With block-diagonal NAs, the two survey blocks are not directly anchored to each other.

\pause

The only link is via \textbf{shared species}: the model must estimate one loading $\symbf{\gamma}_j$ that fits both the coverage and frequency observations of species $j$.

\pause

But rotation ambiguity means we cannot guarantee the two blocks are in the same orientation.

\pause

We need an external anchor.

## Model 1: shared species only

```{r}
fit3 <- gllvm(
  y           = Y_joint,
  family      = family_vec,
  Ntrials     = Ntrials,
  num.lv      = 2,
  zeta.struc  = "common",
  row.eff     = ~(1|site),
  studyDesign = data.frame(site = physical_site)
)
```

Diagnose alignment: cosine similarity between $\hat{\symbf{\gamma}}_{j,\text{COV}}$ and $\hat{\symbf{\gamma}}_{j,\text{FREQ}}$ for each shared species.

\pause

A bimodal distribution at $\pm 1$ signals rotation ambiguity. Non-bimodal signals real disagreement.

## Model 2: spatial anchor

4 coverage--frequency plot pairs lie within 6 m of each other. The spatial covariance provides a partial anchor via nearby plots.

```{r}
fit4 <- update(fit3,
  distLV        = coords_sites,
  lvCor         = ~corExp(1|site),
  studyDesign   = data.frame(site = physical_site),
  Lambda.struc = "UNN")
```

\pause

\footnotesize \texttt{Lambda.struc = "UNN"}: sparse nearest-neighbour Cholesky approximation; see computational considerations slide.

## Results: spatial model

Procrustes comparison of coverage and frequency loadings:

- Correlation $\approx `r pr_cor`$, protest $p = `r pr_p`$
- Most shared species align well

\pause

Fitted spatial range: $\hat{\rho}_{\text{LV1}} \approx `r round(rho_m[1])`$ m, $\hat{\rho}_{\text{LV2}} \approx `r round(rho_m[2])`$ m.

Effective range ($\text{Cor} < 0.05$): $\sim`r eff_m[1]`$ m and $\sim`r eff_m[2]`$ m.

\pause

Most inter-plot distances exceed 80 m; the community gradient is driven by local habitat conditions, not broad spatial autocorrelation. The few close pairs provide just enough anchor.

## Which species disagree?

Species with cosine similarity near $-1$ are the interesting ones:

\pause

- *Erica herbacea*: calcicole specialist, sensitive to management changes
- *Molinia caerulea*: competitive graminoid, potentially expanding since the 1980s

\pause

Disagreement is concentrated in species that have \textbf{changed between the survey periods} (1984--1993 vs.\ 2003--2018), not random noise.

This is a resurvey: disagreement = ecological change, not methodological failure.

## Model 3: adding temporal structure

Year as a concurrent covariate; site random intercepts carry over from fit4:

```{r}
fit5 <- update(fit4,
  num.lv        = 0,
  X             = X_joint,
  num.lv.c      = 2,
  lv.formula    = ~ Year,
  randomB       = "LV",
  lvCor         = ~corExp(1|site),
  Lambda.struc = "UNN")
```

## What does each component do?

- `lv.formula = ~ Year`: LVs are driven by survey year; temporal community change is captured in the ordination axes
- `row.eff = ~(1|site)`: site-level random intercepts absorb overall abundance differences across plots
- `lvCor = ~corExp(1|site)`: residual spatial structure in community composition after accounting for Year

\pause

The residual loadings alignment then answers: after partialling out temporal change, do the two surveys still agree on the community gradient?

## Three model perspectives

\begin{table}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{p{2.0cm}p{2.8cm}p{1.8cm}p{2.3cm}}
\toprule
Model & Anchor & Alignment & Interpretation \\
\midrule
fit3: shared species & Shared $\symbf{\gamma}$ only & Bimodal $\pm 1$? & Rotation ambiguity \\
fit4: + Spatial & Nearby cross-survey pairs & $r \approx `r pr_cor`$ & Methods agree spatially \\
fit5: + Year & Space + time & $r \approx `r pr_cor_5`$ & Residual agreement \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\pause

The three models are not competitors: they answer \textbf{different questions} about the same data.

\pause

The joint family GLLVM makes all three possible within a single framework.

## Model comparison

```{r}
AIC(fit3, fit4, fit5)
```

```{r aic-out, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
print(aic_tab)
```

\pause

AIC favours the more complex models, but the models target different questions: do not use AIC to choose among them.

## Summary

\footnotesize

**Mixed responses**

- `family` accepts a vector; each species gets its own distribution and link
- Shared LVs connect all species into one ordination space
- Enables joint modelling across datasets with different measurement scales

\vspace{0.3em}

**Spatial and temporal autocorrelation**

- `lvCor` and `row.eff` accept structured covariance models (`corExp`, `corAR1`, ...)
- `distLV` provides coordinates for spatial kernels
- Short fitted ranges are informative, not a failure

\vspace{0.3em}

**Combining both**

- Mixed responses + spatial LVs + concurrent ordination: all composable in `gllvm`
- The Garchinger example shows how far this can be pushed on real data

\normalsize
